A user prefers AWS OpenSearch because they don't have to pay for basic features like security and alerts. They call Elastic's paid tiers 'gouging' and 'nickel and diming', and say AWS gives teams the whole Elastic experience without that.

In one commenter's experience, managers, developers and sysadmins all prefer OpenSearch: 'Everyone hates the support and enterprise licensing model.' They already pay for AWS support, so they see no reason to add another vendor.
A commenter says Elasticsearch beats OpenSearch by a wide margin on every metric they checked: GitHub stars and star growth, commits, PRs opened and merged, issues, and Stack Overflow questions.
A commenter who talks to many security teams says new projects generally prefer OpenSearch because of openness, and many teams (e.g., MSPs) are migrating to it.
Two security approaches for Elasticsearch: upgrade to a paid Elastic cluster with its security suite, or put a reverse proxy such as nginx in front to handle security.
Indexing tip: the default refresh interval is 1 second. Raise it if your application allows, and consider disabling it entirely during bulk indexing.

A commenter cites Aphyr's Jepsen analysis showing Elasticsearch could lose indexed documents during network partitions (on an older version). They don't fully trust Elastic's resiliency docs given past handling: 'Elastic is great as a search index, not as a primary database.'
One user found Elastic Cloud on K8s (the operator) to be the best way so far to deploy and manage Elastic clusters on Kubernetes. It handles deployments, statefulsets and upgrades declaratively.

Another user runs Elasticsearch in a Kubernetes StatefulSet. It works nicely out of the box with headless Services for node discovery, plus a custom preStop hook that blocks until the cluster is GREEN so it doesn't go RED on shutdown.

A user was caught out on Kibana 6.x by assuming the X-Pack trial included login, so they added nginx auth. X-Pack security later became free in v7, but since it isn't open source they kept the nginx auth.

Users found the X-Pack tiers and security docs confusing. The subscriptions page didn't make clear what 'File and Native Authentication' meant, and older docs said 'there is no security', which conflicted with free Basic-tier auth.
'Elastic's SaaS offering is incredibly expensive vs AWS Elasticsearch.'
Having used AWS Elasticsearch, a commenter says it has 'a lot of deep problems' in its current state, so Elastic can compete on value.
'The AWS version of ES has been abysmal - its only saving grace is that it's in the ecosystem.' The commenter says they were talked into it by a teammate and will never do it again.

A commenter says Elastic's proprietary add-ons (ML, APM, endpoint security, fine-grained access control) differentiate it, but many users don't need any of that and are fine with the formerly-OSS core.
A user wants to support Elastic but will likely move to Amazon's Apache-licensed fork for internal use, because SSPL is incompatible with their company's open source policy.

'Too late, the community all moved over to OpenSearch.' The commenter won't forgive Elastic for locking basic security behind a paid license. They argue many instances were left exposed on the public internet and auth enabled by default would have helped.

An agency uses elastic.co as its top example of a vague website: no client could say what the company provides. They criticize the pricing model and support, and say the docs assume in-depth prior knowledge of the services and server infrastructure.
'Too late. We just deployed a new project with OpenSearch after learning from an Elastic salesperson that their licensing fees would eat up significant portions of the project's profits.'

A user is happy Elastic kept the Elastic License option. In their view it lets them self-host if the vendor folds or raises prices, fix bugs, and add features, which is less restrictive in practice than AGPL.
